# Upgrade EspoCRM

Orchestrates a safe EspoCRM upgrade. The full step-by-step procedure, major-version specifics, troubleshooting, and rollback commands live in the [Administration wiki — Upgrade EspoCRM version](https://github.com/rodekruis/EspoCRM-knowledge-base/wiki/Administration#upgrade-espocrm-version). **Fetch that page at runtime and read it before acting** — it is the source of truth and may have been updated since this skill was written. Any version-specific one-time steps (e.g. those that apply when crossing a major boundary) live there, not here.

You (the agent) **can run the VM/SSH/root commands yourself** (via the connected terminal/SSH session) — `docker`, `command.sh`, editing files on the VM, `mysqldump`, etc. What you **cannot** do are **Azure portal actions** (VM/disk snapshots, managed-DB backups, resizing) and **EspoCRM admin-UI actions** (maintenance mode, cron, rebuild via UI). For those, ask the user to perform them and confirm **before** you proceed. Your job is to **run what you can, delegate what you can't, verify everything, and gatekeep**.

## Golden rules

1. **Delegate + confirm the manual gates — then verify them yourself.** Before each phase, make sure the **Azure** and **EspoCRM-UI** prerequisites for that phase are done — ask the user to do them and confirm, since you cannot. Never advance past a backup or maintenance-mode gate on assumption. The VM/SSH steps you can just run yourself (showing the command and its output). **A user's "done" is a claim, not evidence.** Most delegated gates have a machine-checkable counterpart — check it before proceeding: `maintenanceMode` / `cronDisabled` in `data/config.php` (and its mtime), `bin/command app-check` (v10+ only — on 8.x/9.x the command does not exist, so read the `config.php` flags), the `extension` table. A UI toggle that was never saved, or a save that silently failed, looks exactly like a completed gate until you look.
2. **When in doubt, consult the official docs.** Fetch and cite [EspoCRM documentation](https://docs.espocrm.com/) — especially [Administration](https://docs.espocrm.com/administration/) and [server configuration](https://docs.espocrm.com/administration/server-configuration/) — and the [release notes](https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm/releases) for the exact target version. Never guess version-specific behavior.
3. **Protect customizations.** Review them (see below) and decide whether any must be moved or edited before upgrading.
4. **Verify, then trust.** After the upgrade, confirm the whole application is actually running. If it is not, roll back.
5. **Verify by content, not status codes — and diff against a baseline.** A `200` from `curl` and "containers Up" do **not** prove a working front-end or intact data. Assert on actual asset content and record counts, and compare them to a pre-upgrade baseline — absolute post-upgrade numbers can't detect data loss or newly-broken flows.
6. **Prove the app bootstraps, not just that it answers.** `GET /` is a static file served by the web server and `GET /api/v1/App/user` returns `401` before much of the application loads — **both can pass while every login returns 500.** The minimum evidence that the backend is genuinely alive is `GET /api/v1/Settings` **and** `GET /api/v1/I18n` returning `200`; these are the calls the login screen itself makes. Never report an instance as healthy or "service restored" on the strength of `/` plus a `401`.
7. **Confirm every write actually landed.** The VM's config files are typically root-owned, and an editor or tool can report a successful edit while writing nothing. Before editing, copy the file; after editing, `diff` against that copy and check the mtime moved. Apply the same suspicion to your own commands — assert on the resulting state, not on the absence of an error message. A change you believe you made but didn't is more dangerous than one that fails loudly.
8. **Reading proves nothing about writing.** Record counts, `GET` endpoints, `app-check`, container status and log greps are all **read** paths — an instance can pass every one of them while every *save* fails. A major upgrade can tighten a formula function, a validator or a hook so that it now throws where it previously returned null, and that surfaces only when a record is written. Do not report an upgrade as verified until you have actually **saved a record** on each customised entity (see Phase 3). This has happened: a 9.1.1 → 10.0.6 upgrade passed the entire read-only checklist while creating a record failed on a before-save formula.
9. **A backup is not a backup until you have asserted its contents.** `mysqldump`/`mariadb-dump` can exit non-zero and still leave a large, plausible-looking file. Check the exit status — and note that `dump | tee file` returns *tee*'s status, not the dump's, so use `PIPESTATUS` or redirect instead of piping. Then assert the file actually ends with `-- Dump completed`. An unverified dump is the one thing whose failure you discover only when you need it.
10. **Treat database connection settings as user-owned and protected.** Never change, normalize, regenerate, or copy database settings between files without the user's explicit consent for the specific proposed change. This includes every `ESPOCRM_DATABASE_*` variable in the Compose file and every setting under `database` in `data/config-internal.php` (including `password` and `dbname`). Before any such edit, identify the exact file and setting, describe the proposed change without exposing secret values, and ask permission. No response or general upgrade approval is consent to change these settings.
11. **The page is not the site — prove the front-end over HTTP, through the web server.** Comparing files on disk with the image proves nothing about what nginx can serve. Fetch the index page, extract every `client/...` asset it references, request each one through nginx and require `200` for all of them, then compare the served `espo-main.js` with the image copy. This has happened: after a front-end refresh every file on disk was byte-identical to the image, while a folder-permission change made nginx return `403` for every JS/CSS/font file and users got a blank page. Re-run this check after anything that touches `client/` or `public/`.
12. **Never print secrets.** The compose file (`MARIADB_*` and `ESPOCRM_*` passwords), `data/config-internal.php` and custom service classes can contain credentials, and anything you print ends up in the session transcript. Don't `cat`/view these files whole: grep for the specific non-secret keys you need, pipe through a redacting filter (e.g. `sed -E 's/((PASSWORD|apiKey|secret|token)[^:=]*[:=]>?).*/\1 <redacted>/I'`), and compare secret-bearing lines by hash (`md5sum`) rather than by content. If a secret does get printed, tell the user which one so they can rotate it.

## Procedure

Work through these phases. Track them with a todo list and stop for user confirmation at each gate.

### Phase 0 — Pre-flight (run what you can, delegate the rest)

The items below marked **[Azure]** or **[EspoCRM]** you cannot do — ask the user to do them and confirm. The **[VM]** items you can run yourself via the terminal.

- [ ] Target version chosen and its [release notes](https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm/releases) reviewed for breaking changes.
- [ ] Does the jump cross a **major** boundary (e.g. 9.x → 10.x)? If so, the one-time steps in the procedure's *Major version upgrades* section on the wiki apply — read them before continuing.
- [ ] **Plan the version steps with explicit image tags — one tag per step.** For a jump across more than one major version, don't let the floating `fpm` tag carry you to the newest release in one go. Set an explicit tag (e.g. `9.0.8-fpm`), upgrade, run the whole of Phase 3 (including the write test), and only then set the next tag. The wiki records which steps are mandatory — e.g. 8.x instances with Advanced Pack **must** go through 9.x, because the extension version v10 requires can only be installed on 9.x. Explicit tags also make rolling back one step a one-line change.
- [ ] **[VM]** Passwordless sudo works: `sudo -n true`. Without it you cannot edit the root-owned compose file, clear `data/cache` or run `command.sh`, and you cannot type the user's password. If it fails, ask the user to set it up as described in the wiki's *Upgrade - with skill* section, then re-check. On Azure, `/etc/sudoers.d/waagent` overrides any rule file that sorts before it, so the file must be named e.g. `zz-…`. At the end, remind the user to remove it, and confirm afterwards that `sudo -n true` fails again.
- [ ] **[VM]** Enough disk space on the VM — run `df -h` yourself. Budget **per version step**: every `command.sh upgrade` writes a full archive to `/var/www/espocrm-backup`, plus the SQL dump you take yourself, so a two-step upgrade needs roughly twice that.
- [ ] **[EspoCRM]** **Maintenance mode enabled** — ask the user (Administration > Settings).
- [ ] **[Azure]** **VM backup** taken — ask the user.
- [ ] **[Azure]** **Database backup** taken, if an external managed DB is used — ask the user (for a self-managed DB you can take the dump yourself, see below).
- [ ] **[VM]** PHP version compatible with the target release — you can check on the VM.
- [ ] **[VM]** **Every installed extension meets the target version's compatibility floor.** Read the installed set from the database (`SELECT name, version, is_installed FROM extension WHERE deleted=0`) and check each one against the target release. **These floors are routinely undocumented by the vendor** and surface only as a migration abort, so treat the wiki's recorded version notes as authoritative and check the vendor's changelog for anything else. Do this *first*: updating an extension requires a working admin UI, so it is far cheaper now than after a failed migration has put the app into a restart loop. **If you update an extension here, re-capture the baseline afterwards** — you have just changed one of the things Phase 3 diffs. **Also check that the required extension version can be installed on the version you are coming from** — it may require the very version you are upgrading to (Advanced Pack 3.13.x requires ≥ 9.0, so from 8.x it cannot be installed first). Then follow the path recorded on the wiki. Don't improvise an extension uninstall or reinstall: an interrupted extension install can leave the old version uninstalled. So the *check* comes first, but the **[Azure]** VM backup and the database dump below must be done before the user actually installs, updates or removes an extension.
- [ ] **[EspoCRM]** **Cron disabled** — ask the user (Administration > Settings).
- [ ] **[VM]** **Capture a verification baseline** (so Phase 3 is diffable). Save to the backup dir: exact `COUNT(*)` (`deleted=0`) for key + custom entities, the count of failed BPMN flow nodes, installed extension names/versions/`is_installed`, and the size/hash of a served front-end asset. Counts and flow-failures are meaningless without a "before". **Then read the baseline back and confirm every section is actually populated** — particularly that the custom-entity list is non-empty. A quoting bug in the collection script yields an empty section rather than an error, and a baseline that captured nothing makes the Phase 3 diff look perfectly clean.
- [ ] **[VM]** **Record the resolved image tags/digests** of every service in the compose file (`docker inspect <container> --format '{{.Config.Image}} {{.Image}}'`). Services pinned to floating tags such as `nginx`, `mariadb:latest` or `certbot` are silently upgraded by the `docker compose pull` inside `command.sh upgrade` — a database or web-server major version can move without anyone deciding to. Capturing this before and after makes that drift visible instead of accidental, and tells you whether a post-upgrade problem came from EspoCRM or from an infrastructure image that moved underneath it. **Record every service, not just `espocrm`** — the one you skip is the one that moves.
- [ ] **[VM]** **Better still, pin the infrastructure tags before upgrading — to a supported release line, not to the running build.** Observing drift after the fact is weaker than preventing it. Replace `mariadb:latest` / `nginx` with a **release-line tag**: `nginx:stable` (or a supported `1.30` / `1.31` line), and `mariadb:<major.minor>` of a **supported LTS line** (e.g. `mariadb:11.8`). Never pin to an exact build or an end-of-life line, as in `nginx:1.27.2` or `mariadb:11.5.2`. A line tag stops major-version drift but still receives patch releases and image rebuilds on every pull. An exact or end-of-life tag freezes its vulnerabilities for good. **This has happened twice:**
  - Unpinned: a 9.3.9 → 10.0.6 run silently took MariaDB from 12.0.2 to 12.3.3.
  - Pinned to "whatever is running" (`nginx:1.27.2`, `mariadb:11.5.2`) during an 8.4.2 → 10.0.10 upgrade: the pin stopped `command.sh upgrade`'s pull from replacing a two-year-old nginx and an end-of-life MariaDB (11.5, end-of-life since Nov 2024). The next day's security scan flagged High nginx/OpenSSL alerts on the nginx container.

  Check end-of-life dates before choosing a line (e.g. `curl -s https://endoflife.date/api/mariadb.json`). If the running line is end-of-life, plan an LTS upgrade **upward**: MariaDB doesn't support in-place downgrades, and an upward move is a database engine upgrade (verified dump, cold copy of the data directory, `MARIADB_AUTO_UPGRADE`). Leave the **app** tag floating if `command.sh upgrade` is your upgrade mechanism — that one is meant to move. The exception is a multi-step upgrade (see *Plan the version steps* above): there you set an explicit app tag per step, and return it to floating once you've reached the target. For the bundled MariaDB container, also set `MARIADB_AUTO_UPGRADE: "1"`, so that if the engine ever does change, the vendor-required upgrade runs instead of being skipped (see Phase 3).
- [ ] **[VM]** **Capture a vulnerability baseline for every service image**, so Phase 3 can show the upgrade left the instance no worse (and ideally better):
  - Scan each image with a **pinned** scanner release, e.g. `aquasec/trivy:<x.y.z>`, never `latest`. Ask the user before running it.
  - Don't mount `docker.sock`: it gives the scanner root on the host. Instead `docker save -o <tmp>.tar <image>` and scan the tar read-only (`-v <tmp>.tar:/scan/image.tar:ro ... image --input /scan/image.tar --format json`).
  - Save the CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW totals and the CVE IDs to the backup folder.
  - The scanner's layer cache can reach **~3 GB** and is written as root. Point it at a throwaway directory, remove it afterwards through a container, and check `df -h`.
  - **Trivy does not report nginx's own CVEs:** the official nginx image installs nginx from nginx.org's package repository, which isn't in Debian's vulnerability data. So also record `docker exec espocrm-nginx nginx -v` and compare it with [nginx.org's security advisories](https://nginx.org/en/security_advisories.html). Commercial scanners such as Orca *do* flag them.
- [ ] **[VM]** **Locate the real compose file rather than assuming its name** (`ls /var/www/espocrm/docker-compose.y*`). It may be `docker-compose.yml` or `docker-compose.yaml`, and docs — including this repo's wiki — do not always match the instance. A command that hardcodes the wrong spelling targets a file that does not exist, which tends to fail in confusing ways rather than obviously.
- [ ] **[VM]** **Read the app container's own startup output before choosing the upgrade mechanism** (`sudo docker logs espocrm | head -40`). The image reports whether it considers the installation upgradeable at all, and that determines which mechanism applies — the standard `command.sh upgrade` path, or a one-time migration from the wiki. An instance can sit for weeks on old application code under a much newer image, having quietly declined to upgrade itself; running the standard upgrade there does nothing at all. **Confirm the running application version rather than assuming the image tag reflects it** — with a whole-folder mount the code comes from the host, so the image and the running version can disagree.
- [ ] **[VM]** **Inventory every integration that writes to EspoCRM from outside**, so Phase 3 can test each one through its real path:
  - API users and their `auth_method` (`SELECT user_name, auth_method, is_active FROM user WHERE type='api' AND deleted=0`).
  - The user agents and paths that actually hit `/api/v1/` in the nginx access log. Ignore scanners, which also use `python-requests`.
  - **API Before-Save Scripts** (`beforeSaveApiScript` in `custom/.../metadata/formula/*.json`), and webhooks.
  
  API Before-Save Scripts run **only** for API requests, so neither a UI save nor an internal/system-user write test exercises them. [kobo-connect](https://github.com/rodekruis/kobo-connect/blob/main/docs/EspoCRM.md) setups rely on them, and its submissions fail while maintenance mode is on — tell the user to resend failed submissions from the Kobo REST service log afterwards. Report the inventory to the user, including "none found" — don't skip this silently.

Do not proceed past a backup or maintenance-mode gate until the user confirms the [Azure]/[EspoCRM] items are done. These map to the "Before upgrading" section of the [upgrade wiki page](https://github.com/rodekruis/EspoCRM-knowledge-base/wiki/Administration#upgrade-espocrm-version).

**If EspoCRM uses an external MySQL/MariaDB database** (i.e. not the bundled `espocrm-db` container), also confirm before proceeding:

- [ ] **DB engine + version meets the target release's requirements** — check MySQL/MariaDB min version for the target EspoCRM in [server configuration](https://docs.espocrm.com/administration/server-configuration/) and compare against the running server (you can run `SELECT VERSION();`). A DB too old for the new EspoCRM is a common upgrade blocker.
- [ ] **The DB user has DDL privileges** (CREATE, ALTER, INDEX, DROP). The upgrade runs schema migrations against the external DB; a read/write-only account will fail mid-migration.
- [ ] **A real database backup exists and its method matches the DB host.** Azure Database for MySQL → **[Azure]** ask the user to run portal *Backup and restore*. Self-managed MySQL/MariaDB → you can take the dump yourself: `mysqldump --single-transaction --routines --triggers -u <user> -p <db> > espo_pre_upgrade.sql`. The VM snapshot does **not** cover an external DB. Verify the dump per golden rule 9 before treating this gate as met — `--routines` in particular fails outright when the engine has a pending `mariadb-upgrade`, which is exactly the situation where you most need a working backup.
- [ ] Note the exact DB host/name/user from `data/config.php` so the same target is used for backup and any restore.

### Phase 1 — Review customizations

This repository's customizations all live under `custom/` and `client/custom/`, which are the folders EspoCRM preserves across upgrades. Still, review them against the target version before upgrading:

- Back-end: `customization/duplication/`, `customization/globalFilters/`, `customization/fieldValidation/`, `customization/entities_nondeletable.md`, `customization/conditionalOptions/`.
- Client-side JS overrides (e.g. `client/custom/src/views/fields/phone.js`) that **extend core views** are the most fragile — a core view renamed or refactored in the new version can silently break an override. Check the target version's front-end for the parent views being extended.
- Metadata JSON under `custom/Espo/Custom/Resources/metadata/` (recordDefs, selectDefs, clientDefs, entityDefs) — confirm the keys/format are still valid for the target version.
- **Formula scripts** — before-save/API scripts under `custom/.../Resources/metadata/formula/`, and the same path inside any extension module (`custom/Espo/Modules/<Module>/...`), which is easy to miss because it is not where Entity Manager writes. Major versions tighten formula functions: an out-of-range or null-ish argument that used to return `null` can start throwing, and because a thrown error aborts the whole before-save script, **the entire save fails**. Grep the scripts for array/string indexing and other operations that assume data is present, and check the target version's implementation of those functions. Concretely, in v10 `array\at` throws on a non-existing index where 9.x logged and returned `null`.
- **Custom PHP — all of it, for every version step, not just the target.** That means hooks, services, controllers, select classes and anything else under `custom/Espo/Custom/`, not only `Classes/`. Major versions remove deprecated base classes and member access, and custom code that still uses them is **not** caught by the upgrade — it fails at runtime, when a hook runs on save or a controller action is called. Run the scan from the wiki's *Custom PHP code: classes removed in 9.0 and 10.0* section (one grep for custom code, one for extension modules) and check every hit against the source of the version you are stepping to. Prefer fixes that also work on the current version (e.g. constructor injection instead of `extends \Espo\Core\Hooks\Base`). Apply those **before** upgrading and save-test them on the old version. Apply a fix that only works on the new version together with the image switch. If the files belong to an extension (`file_list` in the `extension` table), tell the user the fix must also go into the extension's source, or the next reinstall reverts it.

Decide per customization whether to (a) leave as-is, (b) edit for the new version now, or (c) temporarily move aside and re-apply after. Tell the user your recommendation and get agreement before upgrading. When unsure whether an API changed, consult the [Development docs](https://docs.espocrm.com/development/).

### Phase 2 — Run the upgrade

Follow the *Upgrade* and, if applicable, *Major version upgrades* sections of the [upgrade wiki page](https://github.com/rodekruis/EspoCRM-knowledge-base/wiki/Administration#upgrade-espocrm-version). These are SSH/root actions on the VM — **you can run them yourself**. Run each command, show its output, and check the upgrade log (`sudo docker logs espocrm --tail 100 -f`) before continuing. Before running the upgrade, re-confirm the user has done the **[Azure]** backup and **[EspoCRM]** maintenance-mode gates from Phase 0.

For a major jump, complete the one-time steps in the wiki's *Major version upgrades* section exactly as written — do not skip them, and do not substitute a plain `docker restart` for any step that requires re-reading the compose file. Some major upgrades also leave the web-server-served front-end stale even though the backend responds; the wiki documents when and how to refresh it. Verify the outcome by content in Phase 3 rather than assuming the command finishing means success. If an extension version blocks the upgrade, **classify the failure before choosing a recovery path** (see Phase 4) — a migration that aborts before touching the schema does not need a full restore.

**Changing the image version and changing the mount layout are one atomic step, in both directions.** A major release can change what the image contains — e.g. whether the application itself ships inside it — so the compose mounts that are correct for the new version may be wrong for the old one and vice versa. If you move the image tag, move the mounts with it in the same edit, then recreate the containers (`command.sh stop` / `start`), then re-verify. The wiki holds the per-version mount specifics.

**Read the wrapper script before sequencing around it.** `command.sh` is a thin shell wrapper — open it and find out what the action you are about to run actually does, rather than inferring it from the name. Knowing that `upgrade` is `docker compose pull` followed by `docker compose up -d` (i.e. it *does* re-read the compose file) changes the safe ordering of a mount migration: edit the mounts **first**, then run `upgrade`, and the new image and the new mounts land together in a single container recreation. Following a doc that says "edit the mounts, then `stop` / `start`" literally is dangerous whenever the image tag is **floating** (e.g. `:fpm`) and nothing has been pulled yet — `start` brings the containers back on the **old cached image with the new mounts**, which is exactly the crash-loop the docs warn about elsewhere. Verify the file you edited is the one the wrapper uses.

**Database settings are not part of an upgrade edit.** Do not change any `ESPOCRM_DATABASE_*` Compose variable or any setting under `database` in `data/config-internal.php` as part of upgrade preparation, migration, troubleshooting, or rollback unless the user has explicitly approved that exact change. In particular, do not infer or copy `dbname`, `password`, or other values from one file to the other. If the user approves a Compose password edit and its literal value contains `$`, write each literal dollar sign as `$$` in the Compose value so Compose passes a single `$` to the container. Keep the corresponding password in `config-internal.php` unchanged; a `$` is literal inside a correctly single-quoted PHP string. Preserve the existing database name, user, host, and other settings. After an approved change, verify the effective value without printing or logging the secret.

**Clear `data/cache` whenever you change the code version, in either direction.** `data/` is shared with the host and survives an image change, so a cache generated by one version can be read by another and reference classes that don't exist there — which typically surfaces as a 500 on login rather than an obvious upgrade error.

**Confirm the upgrade actually ran — `command.sh upgrade` exiting 0 proves nothing.** Read `docker logs espocrm` until you see the completion line (`Upgrading is finished. EspoCRM version is X` on 9.x, `Completed.` after the migration list on v10), and check the version (`data/config.php` before v10, `bin/command version` from v10). `command.sh upgrade` recreates the database container at the same moment as the app, so the app's upgrade can run before the database accepts connections. It then logs `Upgrade error ... SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] Connection refused` and **starts the old version**, and the site keeps working, so nothing looks wrong. If you see this, confirm the DB is up, `docker restart espocrm`, and read the log again. Likewise, an upgrade that logs `Reverting...` has rolled itself back: read the error, classify it per Phase 4, and don't report progress.

**Step through the planned versions one at a time.** After each step, run the whole of Phase 3, including the write-path check and a fresh baseline, before setting the next image tag. Each step can break something different: classes removed in 9.0 fail at a different point than those removed in 10.0.

**After any front-end refresh, verify per golden rule 11 before telling the user to look.** The wiki's refresh snippet sets folder permissions explicitly for a reason — `rsync -a` copies the source folder's own permissions onto `client/`.

### Phase 3 — Verify the whole application is running

After the upgrade, confirm the instance is genuinely healthy — **not just "the command finished", and not just an HTTP 200.** Run the VM/log/SQL checks yourself; the browser and admin-UI checks you delegate to the user. Where possible, **diff against the Phase 0 baseline** rather than trusting absolute numbers.

Run this whole phase again after **any** intermediate state change — a revert, an image re-pin, a mount edit, a cache clear — not only once at the end. Every such change is a new deployment and deserves the same evidence. Announcing "service is restored" after a mid-run revert is a completion claim and needs the same proof as the final one.

**Structural (no auth):**
- [ ] All containers up: `sudo docker ps` shows `espocrm`, `espocrm-nginx`, `espocrm-daemon`, `espocrm-websocket` — and `espocrm-db` **only if the bundled DB is used** — with uptimes **growing**, none `Restarting`. (With an **external** DB there is no `espocrm-db`; confirm connectivity via a successful record load or `data/espocrm/data/logs/` instead.)
- [ ] **Containers still `Restarting` after a gate is genuinely clear are usually replaying old failures, not new ones.** `espocrm-daemon` and `espocrm-websocket` gate on `app-check` and exit `0` until it passes; Docker's restart backoff grows to roughly a minute, so they keep exiting well after the cause is fixed. Once `app-check` passes *inside that container*, `docker restart <container>` resets the backoff and they come up immediately — do that before investigating further, and confirm with `docker logs <container> --since 2m` producing **no new** output. Relatedly, a web-server reload failing with `host not found in upstream` is a *symptom* of such a gated container being down, not a separate fault; clear the gate, then reload.
- [ ] **Application bootstraps:** `GET /api/v1/Settings` and `GET /api/v1/I18n` both return `200`. These exercise the PHP app end-to-end; `GET /` and a `401` from `/api/v1/App/user` do not (see golden rule 6). If either returns 500, read `data/espocrm/data/logs/` — the class or file named in the `CRITICAL` usually identifies the cause.
- [ ] `sudo docker exec espocrm-daemon bin/command app-check` → migration / DB / maintenance / cron all `OK`; `command.php rebuild` exits 0. (`app-check` exists from v10 only; on an intermediate 8.x/9.x step, check the `config.php` flags and the rebuild instead.)
- [ ] **The data tier is in a complete state — `app-check`'s `Database: OK` does not prove this.** Diff every service's image digest against the Phase 0 baseline. If the database image moved, the engine may now be running against system tables from the previous version: the official MariaDB container **detects that an upgrade is required and skips it** unless `MARIADB_AUTO_UPGRADE` is set, logging `MariaDB upgrade ... required, but skipped` at startup and otherwise behaving normally. Confirm explicitly rather than inferring:
  ```
  sudo docker exec espocrm-db sh -c 'mariadb-upgrade --check-if-upgrade-is-needed -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD"'
  ```
It should report that the installation is already upgraded. If it reports a version jump and "Check required!", take a backup and run `mariadb-upgrade`, then re-check. Do not infer upgrade state from an upgrade-info file; its name and presence vary by MariaDB version. **`MARIADB_AUTO_UPGRADE` only upgrades the system tables** (its log says `user tables won't be touched`), so after any engine change also check the application tables, read-only. Every table should report `OK`:
  ```
  sudo docker exec espocrm-db sh -c 'mariadb-check --check-upgrade --databases espocrm -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD"'
  ```
- [ ] **Security posture is no worse than before — compare by CVE, not by alert count.**
  - Rescan every service image the same way as the Phase 0 vulnerability baseline. Each service's CRITICAL+HIGH total must be at or below its baseline.
  - `nginx -v` must be at least the newest fixed version on nginx.org's security advisories page.
  - The MariaDB line must not be end-of-life.
  - If any of these fails, move that infrastructure image to a current build within (or onto) a supported release line, recreate only that service (`docker compose up -d --no-deps <service>`), and run this phase again.
  - Tell the user that scanners like Orca key alerts to the container: **recreating a container can reopen alerts that already existed** and make them look new. Compare CVE IDs and image digests against the baseline, not alert counts.
- [ ] No *new* `ERROR|CRITICAL` in `sudo docker logs espocrm --tail 100` or in `data/espocrm/data/logs/` since the upgrade timestamp (watch especially for DB/migration errors when the DB is external).
- [ ] `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM job WHERE status='Failed' AND modified_at > <upgrade_ts>` = 0.

**Front-end parity (a `200` does not prove the UI works):**
- [ ] Every asset the index page references returns `200` **through nginx**, and the served `espo-main.js` matches the image copy (golden rule 11). A host-vs-image file comparison is not a substitute: it passes when nginx cannot read the files. If assets are stale, apply the refresh documented in the wiki's *Major version upgrades* / *Troubleshooting* section. If they return `403`, check folder permissions (see the wiki's *Blank page* entry). Then re-check over HTTP.

**Data + functional (diff vs Phase 0 baseline):**
- [ ] Exact `COUNT(*)` (`deleted=0`) for key + custom entities **≥ baseline** (no data loss). Use `COUNT(*)`, not `information_schema.table_rows` (an estimate).
- [ ] Extension rows unchanged and `is_installed=1`.
- [ ] **After maintenance mode is disabled and cron is re-enabled (see Delegate below), prove cron is executing:** Read the `job` table's `Success` count twice a short interval apart and confirm it **increased**. `cronDisabled => false` records intent; a rising counter is the only proof the daemon is actually working through the queue.
- [ ] Authenticated API smoke test with a stored read-only API key: `GET /api/v1/<Entity>?maxSize=1` → `200` for a core entity **and** each custom entity/controller (proves ACL + record load, not just routing). If no such key exists on the instance, **say so explicitly and delegate the equivalent check to the user** — do not silently drop this item, and do not let the unauthenticated checks stand in for it.
- [ ] **Write-path check — mandatory, and not substitutable by any read.** Every item above is a read; all of them can pass while saving is broken (golden rule 8). **Save a record on each customised entity** and confirm it persists. Prefer creating a record with *optional fields left empty* — that is the path that exposes newly-strict behaviour, since populated test data tends to satisfy the assumptions the old version let slide. If you cannot write via API, delegate it explicitly and **do not report the upgrade as verified until someone has**. When stepping through several versions, do this **after every step**: on an 8.4.2 → 9.0.8 step, the only thing that exposed a broken custom hook (`$entity->id` became protected) was saving a record. Clean up after yourself: remove the test records **and** the rows that saving them created in other tables (phone numbers, email addresses, team links), then confirm the counts match the pre-test baseline.
- [ ] **Then read the application log for the write window**, not just for the upgrade window: `data/espocrm/data/logs/`. A failed save is logged as `CRITICAL` there while the HTTP layer, containers and `app-check` all stay green. Distinguish real failures from ordinary `(400) Field validation failure` warnings, which are normal when a required field is left empty.
- [ ] **Each integration from the Phase 0 inventory works through its real path** — e.g. one test Kobo submission via kobo-connect (record, attachment, no `CRITICAL` in the log), and one inbound message from a messaging backend. An internal write test does not run API Before-Save Scripts and does not exercise the integration's API key/HMAC login. If you can't trigger an integration yourself, delegate it explicitly and list it as untested in your report. Never use a production integration's credentials for your own tests.
- [ ] **Canary flow**: touch a dedicated test record that fires a known Workflow/BPMN flow; assert its marker field updates within N seconds, and that the failed-flow-node count **did not increase** vs baseline (pre-existing failures are OK; *new* ones fail the upgrade).

**Delegate (UI):**
- [ ] The web UI loads and login works (not blank / not 404), verified in a **fresh/incognito browser** — **[EspoCRM]** ask the user (or a browser tool if available).
- [ ] **[EspoCRM]** Maintenance mode **disabled** and cron **re-enabled** — ask the user. **The moment they confirm**, verify both flags in `config.php`, then restart `espocrm-daemon` and `espocrm-websocket` and reload nginx without waiting for Docker's backoff (see *Containers still `Restarting`* above). Until you do, live updates fail and nginx logs `502` for `/wss`, which users see as a degraded site right at go-live.
- [ ] A quick functional smoke test: open a record, run a saved flow, confirm customizations still behave — **[EspoCRM]** ask the user.
- [ ] Browser cache/data cleared to rule out stale front-end assets.

If something is broken, first try the matching entry in the procedure's **Troubleshooting** section on the wiki.

### Phase 4 — Roll back if it cannot be made healthy

**First classify the failure — it decides how heavy the recovery needs to be.** Read the upgrade log and establish whether the database schema was actually migrated:

- **Schema not yet touched** (e.g. the run aborts during *prepare* migrations, or refuses to start on a compatibility/PHP gate). The database still matches the old code, so the cheapest correct recovery is to **put the image tag back to the last-good version — together with the mount layout that version requires — clear `data/cache`, recreate the containers and re-verify Phase 3.** No restore needed. Prefer this: it is faster, loses nothing, and keeps the instance available while you fix the blocker. It is also often a *prerequisite* for fixing the blocker, since installing or updating an extension needs a working admin UI.
- **Schema already migrated, app unhealthy.** Now code and schema disagree and only a restore can realign them — continue below.

If the application cannot be restored to a healthy state, **revert** using the *Rollback* section: `sudo /var/www/espocrm/command.sh restore "<archive>.tar.gz"`. Confirm the pre-upgrade backup exists before starting any upgrade — a rollback is only possible if Phase 0's backups were taken.

**External DB — critical:** `command.sh restore` restores the app files (and the bundled DB volume) but does **not** touch an external database. By the time you roll back, the upgrade has already migrated the external schema, so restoring files alone leaves **old code against a new schema** — a broken, inconsistent state. You must restore the external DB **as well**, to the same pre-upgrade backup, so code and schema match:

- Azure Database for MySQL → portal *Backup and restore* (point-in-time / the pre-upgrade backup).
- Self-managed → re-import the dump, e.g. `sudo /var/www/espocrm/command.sh import-sql "/path/to/espo_pre_upgrade.sql"`, or `mysql -u <user> -p <db> < espo_pre_upgrade.sql`.

Restore files and DB from the **same point in time**, then re-verify Phase 3.

## When things go wrong — escalation strategies

Apply in roughly this order:

1. **Read the logs first.** `sudo docker logs <container> --tail 100`. The error usually names the cause (extension version, mount typo, maintenance mode).
2. **Match a known troubleshooting entry** in the [upgrade wiki page](https://github.com/rodekruis/EspoCRM-knowledge-base/wiki/Administration#upgrade-espocrm-version) before improvising.
3. **Update blocking extensions first.** If the upgrade fails citing an extension version, classify per Phase 4: if the schema is untouched, re-pin the image (plus matching mounts) to restore the admin UI, update the extension there, then retry the upgrade. Only fall back to restoring the pre-upgrade backup if the schema was already migrated.
4. **Upgrade version-by-version instead of one-off.** If a large jump fails or the release notes warn of chained migrations, restore the backup and upgrade **one significant version at a time**, verifying health (Phase 3) between each hop. EspoCRM's own upgrade path historically assumes stepping through majors rather than skipping them — confirm the supported path in the [release notes](https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm/releases) and [docs](https://docs.espocrm.com/administration/upgrading/).
5. **Research current best practice** for the specific error before deeper changes: check the [EspoCRM forum](https://forum.espocrm.com/), the relevant [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm/issues), and the [upgrading docs](https://docs.espocrm.com/administration/upgrading/). Prefer the official/supported fix over ad-hoc edits.
6. **Rebuild after manual metadata/customization fixes:** `sudo /var/www/espocrm/command.sh rebuild` (or Administration > Rebuild), then re-verify Phase 3.
7. **If still broken, roll back** (Phase 4) rather than leaving the instance in a partial state, and report findings so the procedure doc can be updated.

## After a successful upgrade

Consider recording any new lesson (an unexpected extension requirement, a customization that needed editing, a version-specific step that was needed) in the [Administration wiki page](https://github.com/rodekruis/EspoCRM-knowledge-base/wiki/Administration#upgrade-espocrm-version) so the next upgrade benefits — keep version-specific mechanics on the wiki, not in this skill.

Where practical, fold Phase 0's baseline capture and Phase 3's checks into a single `verify-espocrm.sh` run twice (`--baseline` before, `--compare` after) that exits non-zero on any failure — so data loss, a stale front-end, and newly-broken flows are caught by the script rather than reported by a user.
